content.intro: This lesson focuses on professional github actions portfolio. content.why_it_matters: Professional GitHub Actions Portfolio matters because it affects correctness, security, maintainability, or operating cost. A professional portfolio should show the design, code, successful and failed run evidence, security decisions, trade-offs, maintenance plan, and recovery procedure. content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: A professional portfolio should show the design, code, successful and failed run evidence, security decisions, trade-offs, maintenance plan, and recovery procedure. A professional pipeline is evidenced, not merely diagrammed: document decisions, prove success and selected failure paths, trace artifacts to commits, and review security and recovery. The most useful check is one that produces observable evidence and fails clearly when its stated requirement is not met.

items.title: Publishing sample workflow repositories
items.text: Make the workflow contract explicit: identify the event, job runner, inputs, command/action, output, and failure signal. Keep steps small and review the permissions and source of every action.

items.title: Documenting design decisions
items.text: For documenting design decisions, state the expected input and result, identify the relevant workflow field or operational decision, and verify it with a controlled check plus run logs. Document the failure condition rather than relying on the YAML file merely parsing.

items.title: Demonstrating secure CI/CD practices

items.title: Presenting measurable workflow improvements
items.text: Make the workflow contract explicit: identify the event, job runner, inputs, command/action, output, and failure signal. Keep steps small and review the permissions and source of every action.

items.title: Explaining trade-offs in pipeline architecture
items.text: Choose runner labels and access boundaries that match the workload. Self-hosted machines need patching, network segmentation, secret protection, and cleanup; keep untrusted contributions away from privileged persistent runners.

content_blocks.code:
name: Capstone validation outline
on: [push, pull_request]
permissions:
  contents: read
jobs:
  validate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: echo "Run lint, tests, security checks, and build validation"
  release-review:
    needs: validate
    if: github.event_name == 'push' && github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: echo "Review the verified artifact before any protected deployment"
content_blocks.expected_output: The second job is limited to pushes to `main` and waits for validation; it does not actually deploy or release an artifact.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Run on a test branch and verify that the review job is skipped for pull requests and other refs.
content_blocks.reset_steps: A production-ready capstone must add real tests, an artifact handoff, environment protection, rollback, and reviewed publication permissions.

content_blocks.title: Practice and verification
content_blocks.text: Inspect the example and make one focused change related to professional github actions portfolio. Predict the expected result first, then use the run instructions or a static review to check it. Record the difference between your prediction and the actual result. Do not add production secrets or grant write permissions just to make a sample pass.

items.title: Syntax and scope
items.text: Check YAML indentation and confirm whether the setting belongs at workflow, job, or step level.

items.title: Permissions and trust
items.text: Start with read-only access. If the example needs more access, explain the exact operation and reduce permissions again afterwards.

items.title: Evidence
items.text: Use the run summary and first failing step. A green result is meaningful only when the intended checks actually ran.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: You should now be able to explain professional github actions portfolio, read the example, and identify a way to validate it. The wider system goal remains: Plan, validate, document, and present a production-ready automation system.

content.task: Apply professional github actions portfolio to a small workflow change. State the expected result first, validate the configuration, then record evidence from the run or static check.
task_acceptance_criteria: Identify the relevant event, workflow field, runner behavior, or security boundary.
Explain the expected success result and at least one failure or skip condition.
Use least privilege and a disposable/test context; do not include credentials or production resources.
hints: Start with the key behavior: A professional portfolio should show the design, code, successful and failed run evidence, security decisions, trade-offs, maintenance plan, and recovery procedure.
Inspect the exact event filters, permissions, expressions, inputs, and job dependencies that affect this example.
Compare the observed status and logs with the expected result; distinguish static validation from a real hosted run.
content.expected_output: The expected result is the behavior described here: A professional portfolio should show the design, code, successful and failed run evidence, security decisions, trade-offs, maintenance plan, and recovery procedure. The real result depends on the repository, selected ref, configured permissions, and runner availability.
troubleshooting: If a workflow never starts, verify the workflow is under `.github/workflows/`, the event and filters match, and repository/organization Actions policy allows it.
If a step fails, inspect the first failed step, exit code, stderr, installed tool versions, permissions, and runner/network state before retrying.
If a job is skipped or data is missing, inspect `if`, `needs`, outputs, artifact names/paths, and cache keys; jobs do not automatically share filesystems.
common_mistakes: Assuming YAML parsing proves the workflow runs correctly or matches the intended trigger.
Granting broad token permissions, printing environment values, or exposing a secret to untrusted code.
Using a placeholder command as evidence of a real build, test, deployment, or security scan.
summary: A professional portfolio should show the design, code, successful and failed run evidence, security decisions, trade-offs, maintenance plan, and recovery procedure.
A professional pipeline is evidenced, not merely diagrammed: document decisions, prove success and selected failure paths, trace artifacts to commits, and review security and recovery.
Use the provided example as a starting point, replace placeholders with repository-specific checks, and validate both success and expected failure behavior before publication.
